title: Hyperkalemia: thresholds, the ECG, and the order of treatment

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on standard emergency and nephrology teaching, including KDIGO and AHA guidance. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: From what serum potassium is hyperkalemia usually called severe, before any ECG change?
questions.why: Mild is 5.5 to 5.9 and moderate 6.0 to 6.4, but any ECG change makes it severe regardless of the number, and the speed of the rise matters as much as the level.

questions.q: What is usually the earliest ECG change of hyperkalemia?
questions.why: The sequence then runs PR prolongation and flattened P waves, QRS widening, and finally the sine wave that precedes ventricular fibrillation or asystole.

questions.q: Potassium is 7.1 with a widened QRS. What is given first?
questions.why: Calcium stabilises the myocardium within minutes but lasts only 30 to 60 minutes and does not lower potassium. The dose can be repeated if the ECG does not improve.

questions.q: What is the standard dose of intravenous regular insulin for shifting potassium into cells?
questions.why: Given with 25 g of dextrose unless glucose is already high. Five units is used by some for patients with kidney failure, where hypoglycaemia is commoner.

questions.q: For how long after intravenous insulin should glucose be monitored for hypoglycaemia?
questions.why: Delayed hypoglycaemia is common, especially with kidney failure, because insulin clearance is slow while the dextrose is gone in an hour.

questions.q: What nebulised salbutamol dose is used to shift potassium?
questions.why: That is four to eight times the bronchodilator dose. It adds to the effect of insulin and works less well in patients on beta blockers.

questions.q: Which treatments actually remove potassium from the body?
questions.why: Calcium protects, insulin and salbutamol shift for a few hours, and only these three lower total body potassium. Shifting alone buys time and nothing else.

questions.q: When does sodium bicarbonate help in hyperkalemia?
questions.a: When there is a coexisting metabolic acidosis
questions.why: On its own it does little for potassium. It is not a substitute for insulin, and it should not be run in the same line as calcium.

questions.q: An outpatient sample shows potassium 6.2, the patient feels well, and the ECG is normal. What is done before treating?
questions.a: Repeat the sample, checking for haemolysis and drawn without fist clenching
d: Give a potassium binder and recheck tomorrow
questions.why: Haemolysis, a tight tourniquet, and very high white cell or platelet counts all produce pseudohyperkalemia. The repeat sample is the test.
Heparin and potassium supplements are the other common ones. The combination of a renin-angiotensin blocker, spironolactone and an NSAID in an older patient with kidney disease is the classic set-up.

questions.q: Which potassium binder has largely replaced sodium polystyrene sulfonate?
questions.why: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate acts slowly and has been linked to intestinal necrosis. The newer binders are also used long term to keep patients on renin-angiotensin blockers.

questions.q: When is urgent dialysis the treatment for hyperkalemia?
questions.a: Severe hyperkalemia with kidney failure or when medical treatment fails
questions.why: Nephrology is called early in a patient with kidney failure, because the shifting agents wear off in hours and there is no other route out.
